hero.headline: Palm Beach County Commission District 6 race reshuffles as Mayor Sara Baxter returns after reversing congressional bid
hero.teaser: Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter reentered the District 6 Commission race before Saturday's noon qualifying deadline after reversing her decision to run for Congress at President Donald Trump's request.
hero.body:
Mayor Sara Baxter has reentered the race for Palm Beach County Commission District 6 after deciding against running for Congress. She submitted her candidacy before the noon qualifying deadline with backing from President Donald Trump, who reportedly asked her to stay focused on county-level representation. Her decision to reverse course and rejoin the district race has prompted criticism from her opponents, who argue that voters deserve candidates with undivided attention to local concerns.

The other candidates running for the seat have questioned whether Baxter's commitment to the district is genuine. Republican Elizabeth Accomondo expressed skepticism about the timing and reasoning behind Baxter's reversal, calling it nonsensical. Democratic candidate Rudolph Tinker suggested that Baxter's credibility as a Republican candidate has suffered as a result of her flip-flopping on the congressional race. Both candidates emphasized that the election should focus on substantive issues affecting District 6 rather than endorsements from national figures. Accomondo stated that taking care of the community's true needs must come first, while Tinker stressed that his candidacy centers on serving the people rather than political maneuvering.

Fellow Democratic candidates Katherine Waldron and Mario Guzman similarly voiced the importance of focused leadership on local matters. Waldron outlined her priorities as tackling traffic congestion, protecting neighborhoods, ensuring quality education, and managing responsible growth in the district. She indicated her intention to continue presenting her platform directly to voters. Guzman called for a candidate committed to public needs who would bring stability to the county commission and move away from what he characterized as a pattern of negativity in local politics. Both candidates believe voters should ultimately decide who best represents them based on their vision for the district.

Interviews with voters and conversations among all candidates reveal that development, traffic management, and the expansion of artificial intelligence data centers are the primary concerns facing District 6. These issues have emerged as central to the campaign discussion. Baxter responded to her opponents' criticism by asserting that the election should be about people rather than politics. The primary election is scheduled for August 18, with the general election following in November. Voters will have the opportunity to choose among the field of candidates competing for the commission seat during these two electoral contests.

cards.headline: Florida homestead exemption increase could strip $11.86 billion annually from local governments, state economists warn
cards.teaser: State economists revealed Friday that a constitutional amendment increasing homestead exemptions could cost Florida's 67 counties $11.86 billion per year if vot.
cards.body:
State economists revealed Friday that a constitutional amendment increasing homestead exemptions could cost Florida's 67 counties $11.86 billion per year once fully implemented. The Revenue Estimating Conference analysis of HJR 1-F showed the fiscal impact would escalate over time, with local governments losing nearly $5 billion in revenue during fiscal year 2027-28, increasing to $8.775 billion in 2028-29, $9.7 billion in 2029-30, and $10.751 billion in 2030-31. The amendment would raise homestead exemptions to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with further increases tied to the Consumer Price Index. Under the measure, local governments would be restricted to funding public safety, infrastructure, schools, debt service, pensions, and constitutional officers including Elections Supervisors, Clerks of Court, Property Appraisers, and County and City Commissions.

Commuter counties face the steepest proportional losses. St. Lucie County could lose 35 percent of its revenue, while Clay, Baker, Citrus, and Hernando Counties could face losses exceeding 30 percent. Large urban counties would sustain the biggest dollar losses: Miami-Dade would face a $445 million revenue decrease by fiscal year 2028-29, Hillsborough could lose $353 million, Broward roughly $326 million, Duval $277 million, and Orange $253 million. Governor Ron DeSantis argued local governments can absorb the impact, noting local property tax revenue nearly doubled from roughly $32 billion in 2019 to about $60 billion today. School taxes would not be subject to the increased exemption limit and would remain at $25,000.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach motorcyclist killed in Boynton Beach crash Friday morning
cards.teaser: A 28-year-old West Palm Beach man was killed Friday morning in a crash involving a motorcycle and a car at a busy Boynton Beach intersection, according to the P.
cards.body:
A 28-year-old West Palm Beach man was killed Friday morning in a crash involving a motorcycle and a car at a busy Boynton Beach intersection, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. The crash happened around 7:08 a.m. at the intersection of Boynton Beach Boulevard and El Clair Ranch Road. Investigators said Albert Garcia was riding a 2007 Kawasaki Ninja eastbound on Boynton Beach Boulevard at a high rate of speed as he approached the intersection.

At the same time, a 2016 Kia Forte driven by a 39-year-old Boynton Beach man was stopped in the westbound lanes of Boynton Beach Boulevard and attempting to make a left turn onto southbound El Clair Ranch Road. As the Kia began turning left, Garcia applied the motorcycle's brakes but did not have enough time or distance to avoid a collision, according to PBSO. The motorcycle struck the passenger side of the Kia inside the intersection. Garcia was thrown from the motorcycle and landed a short distance southwest of the impact point. Rescue crews transported Garcia to Delray Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. The driver of the Kia was wearing a seatbelt and was not injured. Garcia was wearing a helmet.

cards.headline: Stuart daughter files wrongful death suit after Florida Turnpike crash killed three in St. Lucie County
cards.body:
Angeline Dowdian, 22, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against truck driver Harjinder Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson following an August 12, 2025 crash on Florida Turnpike in St. Lucie County. The collision killed Angeline's mother Faniola Joseph, 37, along with Herby Dufresne, 30, and Rodrigue Dor, 54. The three victims were traveling in a minivan when it became wedged underneath a semi-truck after Singh allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked no U-turn zone.

Angeline lived in another country at the time of the crash and had not seen her mother in six years, though they spoke daily via video calls. On the day of the crash, she missed a call from her mother. "She sent me a voice message. She said, 'Angeline, where are you?' This is the first message I go to every morning," Angeline said through tears. She described her mother as both a parent and sole family support. "She was my mother, my father... the only one in my family. I'm living all alone now," she said. Visa restrictions have prevented her from visiting her mother's grave. Joseph had hoped Angeline would become a nurse and would have turned 38 on May 26, 2026.

Attorney Dax Bello of Stuart law firm Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane represents Angeline, with co-counsel Mark Brumer of Brumer & Brumer. The lawsuit alleges that C.H. Robinson knowingly gave business to White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations in its record. Transportation expert James Lewis has described White Hawk's violations as "very egregious." Bello argues the case is supported by a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims when unsafe drivers are placed on the road. That same broker was involved in the Supreme Court case. "This is not an accident, it's a predictable end," Bello said. He emphasized that brokers and carriers have a responsibility to vet safety records before placing drivers on the road.

White Hawk Carriers has since shut down, though Bello warns the company may reopen under another name, a common industry practice. Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida. Bello, a former homicide prosecutor, is helping Angeline navigate both civil and criminal cases under Marsy's Law, which gives victims' families rights to be heard in criminal proceedings. Angeline said no legal victory will undo her pain. "I don't want nobody suffer like me," she said. "Loss of a mother makes you suffer in a way you want to kill yourself, because my mother was everything to me."

cards.headline: Daughter of St. Lucie County turnpike crash victim files wrongful death lawsuit
cards.teaser: Angeline Dowdian filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the truck driver and freight companies following the August 2025 crash on the Florida Turnpike that killed her mother and two others.
cards.body:
On August 12, 2025, three people traveling for work in St. Lucie County died when their minivan became wedged beneath a semi-truck. The crash occurred when the truck driver allegedly made an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked no U-turn zone. The victims were Herby Dufresne, 30, Rodrigue Dor, 54, and Faniola Joseph, 37. Joseph had been living in Indiana and traveled south to purchase goods for her shop when the tragedy struck.

Angeline Dowdian, Joseph's 22-year-old daughter, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against truck driver Harjinder Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson. The lawsuit alleges negligence and unsafe practices led to the crash. At the time of the accident, Angeline was living abroad and had not seen her mother in person for six years, though they spoke daily through video calls. She missed a call from her mother that day, and the last message she received was a voice recording asking where she was. Angeline says she listens to that message every morning. She described her mother as both parents to her and expressed the emotional weight of losing her only family support system. Visa restrictions have prevented her from visiting her mother's grave.

Angeline is represented by attorney Dax Bello of Stuart Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane, along with co-counsel Mark Brumer. Bello argues that the crash was not accidental but a predictable outcome of negligent business practices. The lawsuit contends that C.H. Robinson, a multibillion-dollar freight broker, continued giving business to White Hawk Carriers despite the company's serious safety violations. A transportation expert described White Hawk's violations as "very egregious." The case is strengthened by a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which determined that federal law does not protect freight brokers from state negligence claims when they place unsafe drivers on the road. Justice Brett Kavanaugh's concurring opinion stated that while not all truck accidents can be prevented, some carriers are known to be less safe, and brokers have responsibility to vet driver records before hiring.

White Hawk Carriers has shut down, though Bello warns the company may reopen under a different name, a common practice in the industry. Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida. Bello, a former homicide prosecutor, is helping Angeline navigate both the civil and criminal proceedings under Marsy's Law, which provides victims' families with rights to be heard and informed in criminal cases. Though no legal victory can ease her pain, Angeline hopes the lawsuit prevents other families from experiencing similar loss. She expressed that her mother worked her entire life to provide Angeline with better opportunities and died in a tragic manner before witnessing her daughter's future or meeting her grandchildren.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds vows to revive property tax amendment through state commission if voters reject it in November
cards.teaser: The leading Republican candidate for Governor said he would use Florida's Taxation and Budget Reform Commission to advance property tax cuts if the November ballot measure fails.
cards.body:
U.S. Representative Byron Donalds said Friday on Fox Business that if HJR 1-F fails to reach the required 60% threshold in November's election, he will use Florida's constitutional Taxation and Budget Reform Commission to advance property tax relief as the state's next Governor. The Naples Republican, who qualified for the race this week with President Donald Trump's endorsement, told viewers the commission would study all taxes and fees with the goal of eliminating homestead property taxes or providing relief to seniors on fixed income and working families. The amendment would raise the homestead exemption on non-school levies to $150,000 next year and $250,000 in 2028.

The Florida Taxation and Budget Reform Commission is scheduled to convene in January for the first time in two decades, soon after the next Governor is sworn in, and could advance an amendment for the 2028 ballot. During the same Fox Business segment, Donalds defended Governor Ron DeSantis against the Wall Street Journal's editorial criticism of the amendment as poorly designed. Donalds countered that property taxes in Florida have doubled over the last decade while seniors remain on fixed income and working families struggle to make ends meet, and that local governments watched these increases occur without taking action.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie teen makes history as first Southeast Youth of the Year from St. Lucie County
hero.body:
Enrique Rosario Liz, the valedictorian at Port St. Lucie High School, has achieved a historic milestone by becoming the first member of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County to receive the Southeast Region Youth of the Year award. This accomplishment marks a significant moment for the organization and the local community. Enrique will now travel to New York City on October 1 to compete for the national Youth of the Year title, representing the Southeast region on the country's biggest stage.

Enrique's path to this recognition demonstrates remarkable personal growth and determination. He arrived in the United States from the Dominican Republic eight years ago without knowing English. Rather than letting this challenge hold him back, he actively sought support from his school and the local Boys & Girls Club, using every opportunity available to develop his skills and knowledge. His commitment to learning and self-improvement ultimately led him to become his high school's valedictorian. Today, he holds both the county and state Youth of the Year titles.

The Youth of the Year program celebrates teenagers who stand out as role models, leaders, and positive forces in their communities. The award specifically honors those who demonstrate academic excellence, strong personal values, and a commitment to serving others. Will Armstead, CEO of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County, highlighted what makes Enrique exceptional: "Enrique's achievement is historic, but his character impresses me most. He's turned challenges into opportunities and advocated for others, all with humility and determination." Travis Leonard, owner of A&G Concrete Pools and a longtime program judge, added that Enrique impressed everyone involved and expressed confidence in his readiness for national competition.

As Enrique prepares for the next chapter of his life, he carries the pride of his family and community with him. This fall, he will attend the University of Florida to continue his education. His parents expressed gratitude both to God and to Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County for the role they played in his development. Enrique himself remains focused on his larger mission: to inspire other young people facing challenges. "I could never have imagined this moment when I was 8 years old," he said after receiving the award. "It's a privilege to share my journey, and I hope it inspires belief in every young person who needs a helping hand and an opportunity."

cards.headline: Delray Beach delays Pride memorial honoring Pulse victims amid state restrictions
cards.teaser: Ten years after the Pulse nightclub massacre that killed 49 people, Delray Beach residents are frustrated over obstacles to creating a memorial after the state sandblasted away a rainbow intersection last year.
cards.body:
Friday, June 12 marks 10 years since the Pulse nightclub massacre in Orlando, where 49 people lost their lives. In Delray Beach, a rainbow-painted intersection created to honor the victims was sandblasted away in August 2025 when the Florida Department of Transportation removed it to comply with a statewide push to regulate road markings and remove political and ideological messaging. The state also removed the rainbow crosswalk outside Pulse in Orlando. Other nearby cities took different approaches: Boynton Beach preemptively removed its Pride intersection, while West Palm Beach removed a Pride crosswalk in Northwood but later replaced it with a rainbow corner in a nearby park.

Local advocate Ronnie Dunayer and other residents formed the Delray Beach Pride Memorial Committee and designed a proposal by March for a rainbow pyramid monument etched with the meaning behind each color, to be illuminated at night and honor the victims. Dunayer believes Old School Square would be the ideal location, near the Eagle Scout monument and steps from where the Pride mural once stood. Commissioner Juli Casal identified Senate Bill 1134 as a fresh legal barrier. The bill, which passed 25-11 in the Senate and 77-37 in the House and awaits the governor's decision, would ban local governments from funding or supporting diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives and could put state funding at risk. Casal stated that private funding and private property could allow the memorial to proceed without city involvement.

cards.headline: Hundreds of fish die in Port St. Lucie Sawgrass Lakes community after algae treatment
cards.teaser: Residents of the Sawgrass Lakes community discovered hundreds of dead fish floating in their backyards Thursday morning after the city treated the water for algae earlier in the week.
cards.body:
Hundreds of dead fish were found floating in the Sawgrass Lakes community in Port St. Lucie on Thursday morning after the city hired vendor SOLitude to treat the water for algae on Tuesday and Wednesday. Neighbor Jim Herbert reported seeing "hundreds and hundreds of fish" and "thousands of those little ones just gulping the air." This marks at least the second fish die-off since Herbert has lived in the neighborhood. Experts told WPTV that high heat combined with algae treatment can make water uninhabitable for aquatic life.

On Thursday, Port St. Lucie crews removed the dead fish and tested oxygen levels in the water. Scott Samples with the city said they have been working with neighbors and other cities and counties to find solutions and hopes a couple of options will be available soon. Jim Moir, executive director of the Indian Riverkeeper, recommended the city pursue more natural solutions including planting aquatic vegetation, reducing fertilizer use, and removing sediment that fuels algae growth. Moir warned that without starting with natural remediation instead of chemical treatments, the city will end up in a cycle it cannot break.

cards.headline: Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at St. Lucie County Aquarium marks 25 years in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium on Fort Pierce's waterfront displays fully live models of Florida's coastal habitats, offering visitors close encounters with marine life.
cards.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats through fully live, complex ecosystem models that date back to 1980. Located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce, the facility houses more species than many larger exhibits, including an Atlantic coral reef tank that recreates one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors also see live displays of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities that demonstrate relationships between organisms. Manager Bill Hoffman told WPTV that the aquarium feels like "the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast," and the facility wants to change that perception.

The exhibit's touch tank allows guests to handle unusual marine species under staff guidance, according to exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran. The aquarium will celebrate its 25th anniversary later this year with special programming. Operating in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, the exhibit aims to raise public awareness about threats facing oceans while inspiring conservation. Hoffman emphasized that stable ecosystems depend on many small organisms, a message reinforced throughout the live displays. The facility is open to the public year-round, with more information available at sms.si.edu and on their Smithsonian Marine Station social media channels.

cards.headline: Indian River County faces $50 million budget loss from property tax amendment on November ballot
cards.teaser: Indian River County could lose around $50 million from its $597 million budget if voters approve a property tax amendment on the November ballot, county leaders.
cards.body:
Indian River County leaders gathered Friday at the Heritage Center in Vero Beach to warn the public about a property tax amendment on the November ballot. The amendment would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. According to the Tax Payers Association, the county's $597 million budget could lose around $50 million in funding by 2028. Laura Moss, vice chair of the Indian River County Commission, said the state is dictating how local governments fund operations. Lance Lunceford, president of the Indian River County Tax Payers Association, said there is no way to fill a $50 million hole without reducing law enforcement and first responder services.

Christen Brewer, president of Indian River Firefighters, said fire rescue could lose around $15 to $20 million of their $70 million budget, threatening three projected fire stations. About 79.1% of fire rescue funding comes from ad valorem taxes. Lunceford described the amendment as a tax shift rather than a tax cut, saying the county would likely raise taxes on non-homesteaded and commercial properties to compensate. He warned that increasing taxes on businesses increases costs for everyone through higher prices for goods and services.

cards.headline: Governor DeSantis announces Medicaid fraud crackdown at West Palm Beach press conference
cards.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis announced sweeping Medicaid fraud prevention measures Friday in West Palm Beach, targeting operations officials say have cost Florida taxpayers millions of dollars.
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis announced sweeping Medicaid fraud prevention measures during a Friday afternoon press conference at the Health Care District of Palm Beach County, partnering with President Donald Trump's administration and federal agencies to combat fraud concentrated in southeast Florida. Agency for Healthcare Administration Secretary Shevaun L. Harris revealed that more than a dozen entities presenting themselves as Medicaid providers in West Palm Beach were actually staged operations created solely to steal from the state program. Investigators discovered the fake operations through shared addresses across multiple unrelated entities, suspicious ownership structures, and no evidence of actual patient care.

The state announced three major initiatives to address the problem. The Agency for Healthcare Administration is launching a pilot program with Ventolin, an identity fraud detection company specializing in uncovering sophisticated fraud schemes. AHCA has imposed enrollment moratoriums on high-risk provider categories including durable medical equipment suppliers and adult day care providers. Third, the state is requiring all active Florida Medicaid providers to verify their credentials and identity through comprehensive revalidation. Harris said Florida's program integrity efforts have already saved $136.45 million in recovery and prevention benefits, and over the past two years, AHCA has terminated or denied enrollment to more than 3,200 providers. Florida's Medicaid program covers nearly 4 million recipients statewide.

Manager Bill Hoffman says the facility's philosophy of displaying fully live, complex models of ecosystems dates back to 1980 under the Smithsonian, making it unlike most public aquariums. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman said, noting that more species are housed here than in many larger exhibits.

The highlight is the Atlantic coral reef exhibit, a sprawling tank that recreates one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors will also see live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, each demonstrating the intricate relationships between organisms. The exhibit's touch tank allows guests to handle unusual marine species under staff guidance, according to Chelsie Corcoran, exhibit educator. "You'll likely touch animals you've never seen before," she said.

The facility operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, aiming to raise public awareness about threats facing oceans while inspiring conservation. Hoffman emphasized that stable ecosystems depend on myriad small organisms. The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit is located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce and is open to the public year-round.

cards.headline: Lake Worth woman born without right hand cited by deputy for holding phone she could not hold
cards.teaser: A Palm Beach County deputy pulled over Katie Thomas for allegedly holding her phone in her right hand while driving, but Thomas was born without a right hand. The traffic stop has gone viral with 110 million views.
cards.body:
A Palm Beach County deputy pulled over Lake Worth woman Katie Thomas for allegedly holding her phone in her right hand while driving. The traffic stop has generated 110 million views on social media. Body camera footage shows the deputy telling Thomas what he observed: "You drove past me, holding the phone with your right hand, manipulating that phone. I mean, I saw you." Thomas responded by raising her arm to show her stump. The deputy pressed further, asking multiple times if Thomas had her phone in her hand, and Thomas consistently denied it.

Thomas was born without her right hand and has spent her life as an adaptive athlete, raising awareness for the limb-difference community. "Literally being accused of something that I did not have a limb to be accused. I think that's what's probably one of the most captivating things about the whole thing, is that it was immediate, immediately apparent to 110 million people, that what he claims he saw was impossible," Thomas said. The citation was dropped for lack of evidence. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said an agency review of the case is underway. Thomas harbors no ill will against the sheriff's office and has started selling "Hand to God" merchandise on her Instagram, with proceeds benefiting Shriners Children's Hospital.

cards.headline: Curaçao fans from Port St. Lucie travel to Boca Raton for World Cup team's historic training session
cards.body:
Hundreds of soccer fans filled Florida Atlantic University stadium in Boca Raton on Thursday to witness Curaçao's national team, known as the "Blue Wave," prepare for its historic first-ever World Cup appearance this weekend. The training session drew enthusiastic supporters from across South Florida eager to catch a glimpse of their favorite players before the debut. Goalkeeper Eloy Room spoke with WPTV and said the outpouring of support has fueled the team's excitement. "Really joyful to see that so many people showed up today, it gives us energy. We're really excited to start the World Cup," Room said. Curaçao is the smallest nation to qualify for the tournament, with a population of just over 150,000 people, and went undefeated in all 10 of its 2026 World Cup qualifying matches.

Fans traveled from across South Florida to attend the event, including some who made considerable drives. Marionella Barzeycoggins, a Curaçao native from Port St. Lucie, brought her entire family after learning about the training session. "I found out they're gonna be in Boca and they have a training event. And I'm like, oh my God, I have to RSVP so we are here," Barzeycoggins said. Midfielder Tahitch Chong emphasized the broader significance of the moment. "I think it's amazing to see. The whole world speak highly about Curaçao, just speaking highly about the island is obviously amazing," Chong said. Curaçao faces Germany this Sunday in Houston, Texas, in their opening match.

hero.headline: Humane Society of the Treasure Coast uses Stuart thrift stores to house cats during Palm City shelter renovation
hero.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast shifted many of its cats to two Stuart thrift store locations while adoption, customer service, and intake areas undergo construction at its Palm City shelter.
hero.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two thrift stores to keep animal care going strong during a major renovation of its shelter in Palm City, according to spokesperson Sarah Fisher. The nonprofit began construction on its adoption, customer service, and intake areas earlier this year, temporarily shifting many of its cats to store locations. Senior Manager Kelly Ellis said shoppers can now find not only unique items for sale but also adoptable cats at both thrift stores.

The organization is currently seeking temporary foster homes for other animals while construction continues. The Humane Society's thrift stores are located at 3302 SE Federal Highway in Stuart and 1099 NW 21st St, Stuart. Store hours and donation guidelines are available at hstc1.org.

cards.headline: Smithsonian Marine Exhibit in Fort Pierce offers close encounters with Florida coastal ecosystems
cards.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St.
cards.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce. Manager Bill Hoffman says the facility's philosophy of displaying fully live, complex models of ecosystems dates back to 1980 under the Smithsonian, making it unlike most public aquariums. The facility houses more species than many larger exhibits. The highlight is the Atlantic coral reef exhibit, a sprawling tank that recreates one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors will also see live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, each demonstrating the intricate relationships between organisms, including the aquarium's barracuda that measures just four inches.

The exhibit's touch tank allows guests to handle unusual marine species under staff guidance, according to exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran. Upcoming programming will tie into the facility's 25th anniversary celebration later this year. The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, aiming to raise public awareness about threats facing oceans while inspiring conservation. Hoffman emphasized that stable ecosystems depend on myriad small organisms, a message reinforced by live displays. The facility is open to the public year-round. More information can be found at sms.si.edu and on the Smithsonian Marine Station social media channels.

cards.headline: Delray Beach Public Library launches free summer STREAM programs with daily lunch service for kids and teens
cards.teaser: The Delray Beach Public Library is offering free Science, Technology, Reading, Art, Engineering and Math programs this summer at its facility at Atlantic Avenue and Swinton Avenue, open to all Florida residents.
cards.body:
The Delray Beach Public Library is offering free STREAM programs this summer to kids and teens across Florida. STREAM stands for Science, Technology, Reading, Art, Engineering and Math. The library's 36,000-square-foot facility at Atlantic Avenue and Swinton Avenue welcomes more than 193,000 visitors annually. According to Kae Jonsons, director of development and community relations, the library was founded in 1913 when 30 women from the Ladies Improvement Society each donated a book to start the collection.

Young adult librarian Natalie Baron is directing teen sessions including ColorSpace: Artistic Excavations, where participants explore art history from cave paintings to ancient pottery. Teens can also participate in collaborative 3D puzzle builds and take home themed book boxes. Mandy Fulop, head of the children's department, is launching the STREAM Into Summer Literacy Program, which encourages young readers to set goals with librarians, track progress, and receive an Unearth a Story bag containing a free STREAM book and activities. In partnership with the School District of Palm Beach County, the library serves free lunch daily from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., and snacks from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m., for youth up to age 18. Family Nights on select Tuesdays and Saturday Science Discovery programs for ages 9-12 feature hands-on archaeology activities. Upcoming Thursday evening guests include the Florida Public Archaeology Network on June 11, Sea Turtle Adventures on June 25, the American Shark Conservancy on July 2, and FPAN Beyond Artifacts on July 16. Registration is available at delraylibrary.org.

hero.headline: Congressman Byron Donalds introduces federal bill requiring state and local governments to submit to audits for federal funding
hero.teaser: The Tax Dollar Accountability Act would require governments to open their books to the Comptroller of the Currency, granting total access to records to show compliance with appropriation terms.
hero.body:
U.S. Representative Byron Donalds introduced the Tax Dollar Accountability Act in Congress this week to increase federal oversight of how state and local governments spend federal funds. The legislation would require subsidiary governments to grant the Comptroller of the Currency complete access to their financial records. State and local agencies receiving federal money would need to provide detailed budgets, expenditure reports, vendor contracts, and grant distributions annually to demonstrate they are using appropriated funds in compliance with federal requirements.

Donalds brought forward the bill in response to documented cases of misallocated Medicaid and COVID-19 funding across multiple states. During a Fox News appearance on Saturday, he noted that $200 billion in misallocated payments have already been identified. He argued that any local or state agency receiving federal dollars should make those financial documents available for federal audit at any time. According to Donalds, "I believe local jurisdictions have a responsibility that if you're going to get taxpayer dollars, then your books need to be open and subject to audit by the federal government."

Florida is independently working to combat fraud in its programs. Governor Ron DeSantis announced a Medicaid integrity initiative on Friday designed to strengthen provider screening, use technology to identify fraud, control enrollment for high-risk provider categories, and revalidate existing Medicaid providers. Donalds pledged his support for continuing DeSantis's approach if elected to higher office.

The Naples Congressman vowed to expand these accountability efforts statewide. He stated that his administration would conduct thorough audits of all local governments and state agencies without exception. "We will DOGE all local governments and all state agencies. There will be no sacred cows because the taxpayers deserve to make sure that their dollars are being spent efficiently and transparently," Donalds said. He committed to maintaining these standards of financial oversight and transparency across Florida if he advances in political office.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds vows to revive property tax amendment through state commission if voters reject it in November
cards.teaser: The leading Republican candidate for Governor said he would use Florida's Taxation and Budget Reform Commission to advance property tax cuts if the November ballot measure fails.
cards.body:
U.S. Representative Byron Donalds said Friday on Fox Business that if HJR 1-F fails to reach the required 60% threshold in November's election, he will use Florida's constitutional Taxation and Budget Reform Commission to advance property tax relief as the state's next Governor. The Naples Republican, who qualified for the race this week with President Donald Trump's endorsement, told viewers the commission would study all taxes and fees with the goal of eliminating homestead property taxes or providing relief to seniors on fixed income and working families. The amendment would raise the homestead exemption on non-school levies to $150,000 next year and $250,000 in 2028.

The Florida Taxation and Budget Reform Commission is scheduled to convene in January for the first time in two decades, soon after the next Governor is sworn in, and could advance an amendment for the 2028 ballot. During the same Fox Business segment, Donalds defended Governor Ron DeSantis against the Wall Street Journal's editorial criticism of the amendment as poorly designed. Donalds countered that property taxes in Florida have doubled over the last decade while seniors remain on fixed income and working families struggle to make ends meet, and that local governments watched these increases occur without taking action.

cards.headline: Florida homestead exemption increase could strip $11.86 billion annually from local governments, state economists warn
cards.teaser: State economists revealed Friday that a constitutional amendment increasing homestead exemptions could cost Florida's 67 counties $11.86 billion per year if vot.
cards.body:
State economists revealed Friday that a constitutional amendment increasing homestead exemptions could cost Florida's 67 counties $11.86 billion per year once fully implemented. The Revenue Estimating Conference analysis of HJR 1-F showed the fiscal impact would escalate over time, with local governments losing nearly $5 billion in revenue during fiscal year 2027-28, increasing to $8.775 billion in 2028-29, $9.7 billion in 2029-30, and $10.751 billion in 2030-31. The amendment would raise homestead exemptions to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with further increases tied to the Consumer Price Index. Under the measure, local governments would be restricted to funding public safety, infrastructure, schools, debt service, pensions, and constitutional officers including Elections Supervisors, Clerks of Court, Property Appraisers, and County and City Commissions.

Commuter counties face the steepest proportional losses. St. Lucie County could lose 35 percent of its revenue, while Clay, Baker, Citrus, and Hernando Counties could face losses exceeding 30 percent. Large urban counties would sustain the biggest dollar losses: Miami-Dade would face a $445 million revenue decrease by fiscal year 2028-29, Hillsborough could lose $353 million, Broward roughly $326 million, Duval $277 million, and Orange $253 million. Governor Ron DeSantis argued local governments can absorb the impact, noting local property tax revenue nearly doubled from roughly $32 billion in 2019 to about $60 billion today. School taxes would not be subject to the increased exemption limit and would remain at $25,000.

cards.headline: Republican Lee Steinhauer exits HD 45 race, endorses Orange County GOP Chair Erin Huntley
cards.teaser: The Winter Garden lawyer ended his campaign Friday as the qualifying window closed, clearing Huntley's path to a one-on-one contest with Democratic Rep. Leonard Spencer.
cards.body:
Lee Steinhauer, the Winter Garden lawyer who filed last spring to challenge for the House District 45 seat, ended his campaign Friday and endorsed Erin Huntley, the Orange County GOP Chair who has led the field from the start. Steinhauer announced the decision on Facebook as the qualifying window closed, citing his family and two young sons. "I have two young sons that I want to be there for as they grow up, and while running for political office can wait, their childhoods will not," he wrote. He framed his exit as necessary for Republican unity heading into the general election, calling Huntley "a great candidate" and "a friend I fully endorse."

The withdrawal clears Huntley's path to face Democratic Rep. Leonard Spencer in November, the matchup Republicans have wanted since she filed. HD 45, which sprawls across Orange and Osceola counties, is a priority flip target for Republicans. Spencer unseated Republican Rep. Carolina Amesty by roughly 1,600 votes in 2024, the only race in Florida where a Democrat knocked off a sitting Republican. Huntley filed in January 2025 and raised more than $252,000 by the end of last year while securing endorsements from U.S. Representative Daniel Webster, Senate President Mike Haridopolos, Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson, Attorney General James Uthmeier, and Osceola Sheriff Christopher Blackmon. Governor Ron DeSantis appointed her to the Florida Virtual School Board of Trustees earlier in the cycle. Steinhauer loaned his campaign $20,000 but never closed the money gap.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds unveils Read to Succeed plan to boost childhood literacy across Florida
cards.teaser: The Republican gubernatorial candidate released a plan Saturday that incorporates science-of-reading teacher training, early intervention for K-2 students, and extra tutoring for third graders.
cards.body:
Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds unveiled his Read to Succeed plan on Saturday, which includes science-of-reading-based teacher training, early intervention for K-2 students, extra tutoring for Grade 3 students who need it, and a new statewide Read to Succeed Award for teachers who go above and beyond. Donalds said that when children learn to read by third grade, every door ahead of them is opened, but when they fall behind, those doors of opportunity are closed.

Childhood literacy remains a significant challenge in Florida. The state ranks worse than 44 other states in reading recovery, and 44% of fourth graders cannot read on grade level. Donalds plans to appeal to President Donald Trump and Education Secretary Linda McMahon for Title funding waivers to support literacy programs, including incentives for districts that demonstrate gains. Donalds characterized his plan as empowering parents and teachers with tools, technology, and tutoring rather than imposing a new mandate. He has also made childhood education central to his campaign, advocating for individual learning plans for all students and long-term Student Success Plans beginning no later than sixth grade to help young people prepare for careers.

cards.headline: Senator Rick Scott requests federal probe into California elections after Los Angeles mayoral race
cards.teaser: The Florida Senator sent a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche and Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon urging an investigation into alleged election irregularities in the Los Angeles mayoral contest.
cards.body:
U.S. Senator Rick Scott sent a letter Friday to Attorney General Todd Blanche and Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon urging a probe into alleged election irregularities in the Los Angeles mayoral race, including charges that opposition candidates paid the unhoused to vote. Scott stated that Americans expect and deserve elections that are free, fair, transparent, and efficient, and that California clearly does not want to meet those standards. He cited troubling reports of fraudulent ballots being submitted, people paying homeless people to cast ballots, and delays in ballot counting as reasons for concern.

Scott's letter notes that the U.S. Attorney General's office prosecuted a petition circulator in Los Angeles for allegedly paying people to register to vote using addresses where they did not live, which would compound the fraud if proven true. He added that many Americans do not view this case as an isolated incident but as part of a broader pattern of vulnerabilities that have undermined public confidence in elections. Independent candidate Spencer Pratt fell short of the runoff in the Los Angeles mayoral race. More than half the voters in the city are registered Democrats, while less than 19 percent are Republicans and the remainder are registered independents. Pratt ran as an independent in part because the GOP brand does not help in the city, though his campaign was boosted by Republican politicians like Scott and news outlets including the California Post and Fox News.

hero.headline: Stuart daughter files wrongful death suit after Florida Turnpike crash killed three in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
Angeline Dowdian, 22, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against truck driver Harjinder Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson following an August 12, 2025 crash on Florida Turnpike in St. Lucie County. The collision killed Angeline's mother Faniola Joseph, 37, along with Herby Dufresne, 30, and Rodrigue Dor, 54. The three victims were traveling in a minivan when it became wedged underneath a semi-truck after Singh allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked no U-turn zone.

Angeline lived in another country at the time of the crash and had not seen her mother in six years, though they spoke daily via video calls. On the day of the crash, she missed a call from her mother. "She sent me a voice message. She said, 'Angeline, where are you?' This is the first message I go to every morning," Angeline said through tears. She described her mother as both a parent and sole family support. "She was my mother, my father... the only one in my family. I'm living all alone now," she said. Visa restrictions have prevented her from visiting her mother's grave. Joseph had hoped Angeline would become a nurse and would have turned 38 on May 26, 2026.

Attorney Dax Bello of Stuart law firm Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane represents Angeline, with co-counsel Mark Brumer of Brumer & Brumer. The lawsuit alleges that C.H. Robinson knowingly gave business to White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations in its record. Transportation expert James Lewis has described White Hawk's violations as "very egregious." Bello argues the case is supported by a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims when unsafe drivers are placed on the road. That same broker was involved in the Supreme Court case. "This is not an accident, it's a predictable end," Bello said. He emphasized that brokers and carriers have a responsibility to vet safety records before placing drivers on the road.

White Hawk Carriers has since shut down, though Bello warns the company may reopen under another name, a common industry practice. Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida. Bello, a former homicide prosecutor, is helping Angeline navigate both civil and criminal cases under Marsy's Law, which gives victims' families rights to be heard in criminal proceedings. Angeline said no legal victory will undo her pain. "I don't want nobody suffer like me," she said. "Loss of a mother makes you suffer in a way you want to kill yourself, because my mother was everything to me."

cards.teaser: Ed W Farrell of Jensen Beach has died, according to All County Funeral Home & Crematory.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie teen named Southeast Youth of the Year, heads to national competition
cards.teaser: Enrique Rosario Liz, valedictorian at Treasure Coast High School, became the first member of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County to win Southeast Region Youth of the Year.
cards.body:
Enrique Rosario Liz, valedictorian at Lucie High School in Port St. Lucie, has made history as the first member of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County to be named Southeast Region Youth of the Year. Eight years ago, he arrived from the Dominican Republic without speaking English. Through encouragement from his school and the local Boys & Girls Club, he seized every opportunity to grow and thrive, becoming the county's graduating valedictorian. As both the county's Youth of the Year and Florida Youth of the Year, Enrique will represent the Southeast at the National Youth of the Year competition on October 1 in New York City. This fall, he is headed to the University of Florida.

Will Armstead, CEO of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County, praised Enrique's character and resilience. "Enrique's achievement is historic, but his character impresses me most. He's turned challenges into opportunities and advocated for others, all with humility and determination," Armstead said. Travis Leonard, owner of A&G Concrete Pools and longtime Youth of the Year judge, noted that Enrique stood out from the start. "Thanks to his hard work and all those who support him, we finally have a Southeast Region Youth of the Year," Leonard said. The Youth of the Year program is Boys & Girls Clubs of America's top celebration of teens who serve as role models, leaders, and change-makers in their communities.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach motorcyclist killed in Boynton Beach intersection crash
cards.teaser: Albert Garcia, 28, of West Palm Beach died Friday morning after his motorcycle struck a car at Boynton Beach Boulevard and El Clair Ranch Road.
cards.body:
A 28-year-old West Palm Beach man was killed Friday morning in a crash involving a motorcycle and a car at the intersection of Boynton Beach Boulevard and El Clair Ranch Road, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. The crash happened around 7:08 a.m. Investigators said Albert Garcia was riding a 2007 Kawasaki Ninja eastbound on Boynton Beach Boulevard at a high rate of speed as he approached the intersection.

At the same time, a 2016 Kia Forte driven by a 39-year-old Boynton Beach man was stopped in the westbound lanes of Boynton Beach Boulevard and attempting to make a left turn onto southbound El Clair Ranch Road. As the Kia began turning left, Garcia applied the motorcycle's brakes but did not have enough time or distance to avoid a collision. The motorcycle struck the passenger side of the Kia inside the intersection. Garcia was thrown from the motorcycle and landed a short distance southwest of the impact point. Rescue crews transported Garcia to Delray Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. The driver of the Kia was wearing a seatbelt and was not injured. Garcia was wearing a helmet.

cards.headline: Sara Baxter returns to Palm Beach County Commission District 6 race after congressional reversal
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter reentered the District 6 Commission race after President Donald Trump asked her to remain in Palm Beach County.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter is back in the race for the District 6 Commission seat after reversing her decision to run for Congress. Baxter reentered the race, meeting the noon qualifying deadline, with President Donald Trump's endorsement after Trump asked her to remain in Palm Beach County. However, other candidates say the focus should remain on community needs rather than the endorsement from the White House. Republican candidate Elizabeth Accomondo and Democratic candidate Rudolph Tinker both emphasized that issues facing District 6 should take priority. "What's important is that we take care of the true needs of the community first, first and foremost," Accomondo said. Tinker added, "For me, it's about the people, and if it's not about the people, I'm out."

Democratic candidates Katherine Waldron and Mario Guzman echoed similar sentiments. Waldron stated that District 6 needs focused leadership on traffic, neighborhood protection, quality education, and responsible growth. Guzman said residents deserve a candidate committed to public needs and stability. Across all candidates, the main issues facing District 6 are development, traffic, and the emergence of AI data centers. Baxter responded to the candidates' thoughts in a statement, saying "This election is about people, NOT politics." Voters will decide the District 6 race on Primary Day, August 18, with the general election in November.

cards.headline: Delray Beach memorial committee pushes for Pulse victims tribute amid state restrictions
cards.teaser: The Delray Beach Pride Memorial Committee has designed a rainbow pyramid monument to honor the 49 victims of the Pulse nightclub massacre, but faces obstacles including Senate Bill 1134.
cards.body:
Friday, June 12 marks 10 years since the Pulse nightclub massacre in Orlando, where 49 people lost their lives. A rainbow-painted Pride mural once honored those victims at a Delray Beach intersection, but in August 2025, the Florida Department of Transportation sandblasted it away to comply with a statewide push to regulate road markings and remove political and ideological messaging. Delray Beach initially explored legal action but shelved the idea, citing a potentially costly fight. The city suggested instead putting resources toward creating a new memorial nearly a year ago.

Local advocate Ronnie Dunayer and other residents formed the Delray Beach Pride Memorial Committee and designed a proposal for a rainbow pyramid monument etched with the meaning behind each color, illuminated at night. Dunayer proposes placing it at Old School Square, near the Eagle Scout monument and steps from where the Pride mural once stood. Commissioner Juli Casal identified two legal barriers: Senate Bill 1134, which would ban local governments from funding diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives after passing 25-11 in the Senate and 77-37 in the House, and the challenge of using city money and property. Casal noted that private funding and private property could accelerate the process and could be completed immediately. Dunayer is reaching out to state leaders and national organizations for solutions.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie teen Enrique Rosario Liz makes history as Southeast Youth of the Year, heads to national competition
hero.body:
Enrique Rosario Liz has achieved a milestone for his community. The valedictorian of a local high school has become the first member of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County to win the Southeast Region Youth of the Year award. He will now travel to New York City on October 1 to compete in the national championship. The Southeast Region award recognizes outstanding teens who demonstrate academic excellence, strong moral values, and a commitment to serving others through the Boys & Girls Clubs network.

Enrique's path to this achievement began eight years ago when he immigrated to Port St. Lucie from the Dominican Republic with no English language skills. He credits his school and the local Boys & Girls Club for encouraging him to pursue opportunities and challenge himself. Through determination and support, he has transformed from a newcomer into a leader. His accomplishments include earning county Youth of the Year honors, Florida Youth of the Year recognition, and valedictorian status at his high school. In the fall, he will enroll at the University of Florida to continue his education. When accepting his award, Enrique reflected on his journey, saying "I could never have imagined this moment when I was 8 years old" and expressed hope that his story would inspire other young people seeking guidance and opportunity.

Leaders throughout St. Lucie County have praised Enrique's character and work ethic. Will Armstead, CEO of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County, stated that while the historic achievement is noteworthy, Enrique's character stands out even more. Armstead highlighted how Enrique has converted obstacles into stepping stones and supported others with both humility and resolve. Travis Leonard, an owner of A&G Concrete Pools and experienced Youth of the Year judge, observed that Enrique distinguished himself immediately among competitors. Leonard expressed confidence that Enrique possesses the qualities needed to succeed at the national level and voiced pride in both Enrique and the broader community for their support.

Enrique's family has responded with gratitude for the opportunities their son has received. His parents emphasized their appreciation for both divine blessing and the direct support provided by Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County in helping Enrique develop into both a leader and a well-rounded person. The Youth of the Year program, managed by Boys & Girls Clubs of America, represents the organization's premier recognition of young people who serve as role models and catalysts for change within their communities. Enrique's transformation from a young immigrant to a nationally competitive scholar continues to motivate others throughout St. Lucie County.

cards.headline: 16-year-old charged with attempted homicide after Fort Pierce shooting leaves another teen critically injured
cards.teaser: A 16-year-old was arrested and charged with attempted homicide after a shooting Thursday night on Avenue N in Fort Pierce left another 16-year-old in critical condition.
cards.body:
A 16-year-old has been arrested and charged with attempted homicide after a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce. According to Fort Pierce police, detectives from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office heard gunshots while traveling on Avenue N and observed three juveniles fleeing in different directions. Another juvenile was discovered laying on the sidewalk on top of a bike with gunshot wounds. The 16-year-old victim remains in critical condition at a local hospital as of Friday morning.

Detectives and officers established a perimeter in the area and apprehended all three suspects. One suspect was caught by a sheriff's office K9, while another was found hiding in a recycling container. Two weapons were recovered during the operation. The 16-year-old suspect was charged with attempted homicide, tampering with evidence and unlawful carry of a firearm by a person under 18. He was taken to the Department of Juvenile Justice.

cards.headline: Daughter of Florida Turnpike crash victim files wrongful death lawsuit against trucking companies
cards.teaser: Angeline Dowdian, 22, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit after her mother Faniola Joseph and two others were killed in an August 2025 crash on the Florida Turnpike in St. Lucie County.
cards.body:
On August 12, 2025, Herby Dufresne, 30, Faniola Joseph, 37, and Rodrigue Dor, 54, were traveling for work in St. Lucie County when their minivan became wedged underneath a semi-truck driven by Harjinder Singh. Singh allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked "No U-turn" zone. All three people in the minivan were killed. Singh worked for White Hawk Carriers, a company with a troubling safety record. Joseph's daughter, Angeline Dowdian, 22, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson, alleging negligence and unsafe practices.

Angeline, who lived in another country at the time and had not seen her mother in person in six years, is represented by attorney Dax Bello of Stuart firm Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane, along with co-counsel Mark Brumer of Brumer & Brumer. The lawsuit alleges that C.H. Robinson knowingly gave business to White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations in its record. Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida. White Hawk Carriers has since shut down. The case is bolstered by a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport that clarified federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims.

cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce pastor faces child neglect charges involving five foster children under his care.
cards.body: A pastor in Fort Pierce has been charged with child neglect of five foster children. The charges involve allegations related to the care and supervision of the children who were placed in the pastor's home as foster placements. The case is under investigation by local authorities.

cards.headline: Smithsonian Marine Exhibit in Fort Pierce showcases Florida ocean ecosystems
cards.teaser: A Smithsonian Marine Exhibit in Fort Pierce brings Florida's ocean ecosystems to life for local visitors.
cards.body: The Smithsonian Marine Exhibit in Fort Pierce offers residents and visitors an opportunity to explore Florida's ocean ecosystems. The exhibit features marine life and educational displays highlighting the diverse underwater environments found off Florida's coast. The exhibit serves as an educational resource for the community to learn about local marine habitats.

cards.headline: World Cup watch parties scheduled from Boca Raton to Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: Venues across the region, including Fort Pierce, are hosting watch parties for the 2026 World Cup.
cards.body: Watch parties for the 2026 World Cup are being organized at venues from Boca Raton to Fort Pierce. Local bars, restaurants and community centers are preparing to host gatherings where soccer fans can watch matches together. The World Cup is taking place this summer, and venues across the Treasure Coast are offering viewing opportunities for residents.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie teen named Southeast Region Youth of the Year, competes for national title
hero.teaser: Enrique Rosario Liz, valedictorian at St. Lucie High School, became the first member of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County to win the Southeast Region Youth of the Year award.
hero.body:
Enrique Rosario Liz, valedictorian of St. Lucie High School, has achieved a historic milestone by becoming the first member of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County to earn the Southeast Region Youth of the Year award. He will now travel to New York City on October 1 to compete for the national title in the Boys & Girls Clubs of America's top youth recognition program. The award honors outstanding teenagers across the Boys & Girls Clubs community who demonstrate academic excellence, strong values, and leadership through service.

Enrique's path to this achievement reflects remarkable personal growth and determination. He arrived in Port St. Lucie from the Dominican Republic eight years ago without speaking English. With support from his school and the local Boys & Girls Club, he transformed his circumstances into opportunities for growth. "I could never have imagined this moment when I was 8 years old," Enrique said after receiving the award. "It's a privilege to share my journey, and I hope it inspires belief in every young person who needs a helping hand and an opportunity." His dedication throughout high school culminated in earning the valedictorian position. This fall, he will attend the University of Florida, though he will first represent the Southeast Region at the national competition.

Will Armstead, CEO of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County, praised Enrique's character and impact. "Enrique's achievement is historic, but his character impresses me most. He's turned challenges into opportunities and advocated for others—all with humility and determination." Travis Leonard, owner of A&G Concrete Pools and a longtime Youth of the Year judge, also recognized Enrique's exceptional qualities. "From the start, Enrique stood out. Thanks to his hard work—and all those who support him—we finally have a Southeast Region Youth of the Year. I believe he's ready for the national competition, and I'm proud of him and our whole community."

Enrique's accomplishments have brought pride to his family and community. His parents expressed their gratitude for the opportunities that shaped their son's development. "We're grateful to God for every opportunity and to Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County for helping Enrique grow as a leader and a person," they said. The Youth of the Year program celebrates teenagers who demonstrate leadership and positive impact in their communities, making Enrique's selection recognition of both his individual achievements and his contributions to those around him.

cards.headline: Vero Beach man charged with murder of 76-year-old grandmother who welcomed him into her home
cards.teaser: Nicholas Leonard Ivey, 29, now faces murder charges in the death of Patricia Ann DiBella, who was found dead at her home on Fairways Circle in February.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced Friday that 29-year-old Nicholas Leonard Ivey faces charges of murder and tampering with physical evidence in the death of 76-year-old Patricia Ann DiBella. Investigators said Ivey admitted to killing DiBella, his grandmother, who had opened her home to him at her residence at 5090 Fairways Circle north of Vero Beach. On February 1, a welfare check was requested by family members, which led deputies to the scene the following day, where Ivey was taken into custody. Since February, Ivey has been held on other related charges. The sheriff's office formally charged him with murder on June 3. Ivey is being held at the Indian River County Jail without bond.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said in a statement that no one should lose their life at the hands of someone they trusted and welcomed into their home, and he encouraged anyone experiencing domestic violence to contact law enforcement. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said domestic violence can take many forms and can affect anyone. Anyone in danger should call 911, SafeSpace at 772-288-7023, or the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233.

cards.headline: Indian River County faces $50 million budget loss from property tax amendment on November ballot
cards.teaser: Indian River County leaders warned Friday that a property tax amendment on the November ballot could cost the county $50 million in annual revenue by 2028.
cards.body:
Indian River County leaders gathered Friday at the Heritage Center in Vero Beach to discuss a property tax amendment on the November ballot that could reduce county revenue by $50 million by 2028. The amendment would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Vice Chair Laura Moss convened the meeting with neighbors and community leaders, stating the state is dictating to local governments how to fund services. Lance Lunceford, president of the Indian River County Tax Payers Association, called the amendment "an unsound, unplanned piece of public policy." With the county operating on a $597 million budget, Lunceford said the projected $50 million loss represents a substantial portion of funding with no way to fill the hole without reducing law enforcement and first responder services.

Christen Brewer, president of Indian River Firefighters, said fire rescue could lose $15 to $20 million of their $70 million budget, as 79.1 percent of fire rescue funding comes from ad valorem taxes. Brewer noted three projected stations may not be built if the shortfall occurs. Lunceford characterized the amendment as a tax shift rather than a tax cut, potentially requiring the county to raise taxes on non-homesteaded and commercial properties to offset lost revenue.

cards.headline: Delray Beach memorial committee pushes for permanent Pride monument amid state restrictions
cards.teaser: The Delray Beach Pride Memorial Committee proposed a rainbow pyramid monument to honor Pulse nightclub victims, but new state legislation creates obstacles for city funding and property.
cards.body:
Friday marks 10 years since the Pulse nightclub massacre in Orlando, where 49 people lost their lives. In Delray Beach, a Pride mural honoring the victims was sandblasted away in August 2025 by the Florida Department of Transportation. The state removed the rainbow-painted intersection to comply with a statewide effort to regulate road markings and remove political and ideological messaging. Local advocate Ronnie Dunayer and other residents formed the Delray Beach Pride Memorial Committee to create an alternative memorial.

By March, the committee designed a proposal for a rainbow pyramid monument etched with the meaning behind each color, illuminated at night. Dunayer proposed placing it at Old School Square, near the Eagle Scout monument and steps from where the Pride mural once stood. However, Senate Bill 1134, awaiting the governor's decision, presents a legal obstacle. The bill would ban local governments from funding or supporting diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives and could put state funding at risk if municipalities use city property or dollars for such projects. The bill passed 25-11 in the Senate and 77-37 in the House. Commissioner Juli Casal noted that private funding and private property could accelerate the process. Dunayer is reaching out to state leaders and national organizations to find solutions and bring a tribute to the Pulse victims back to Delray Beach.

cards.headline: Daughter of Florida Turnpike crash victim files wrongful death suit against trucking company
cards.teaser: Angeline Dowdian, daughter of Faniola Joseph, who was killed in an August 2025 crash in St. Lucie County, filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the truck driver and White Hawk Carriers.
cards.body:
On August 12, 2025, Herby Dufresne, 30, Faniola Joseph, 37, and Rodrigue Dor, 54, were traveling for work in St. Lucie County when their minivan became wedged underneath a semi-truck. The truck driver, Harjinder Singh, allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked "No U-turn" zone. All three people in the minivan were killed. Joseph's only child, Angeline Dowdian, 22, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson, alleging negligence and unsafe practices. Dowdian is represented by attorney Dax Bello of Stuart law firm Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane, and co-counsel Mark Brumer of Brumer & Brumer.

Bello argues that C.H. Robinson knowingly gave business to White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations in its record. The lawsuit is bolstered by a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims when unsafe drivers are placed on the road. Singh also faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida. White Hawk Carriers has since shut down, though Bello warns the company may reopen under another name, a practice common in the industry.

cards.headline: Sara Baxter returns to Palm Beach County Commission race after reversing decision to run for Congress
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter reentered the District 6 Commission race after meeting the noon qualifying deadline, with President Donald Trump's endorsement.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter reentered the race for the District 6 Commission seat after reversing her decision to run for Congress, meeting the noon qualifying deadline with President Donald Trump's endorsement. Trump asked her to remain in Palm Beach County. Republican candidate Elizabeth Accomondo and Democratic candidate Rudolph Tinker criticized the move, saying the focus should remain on community needs rather than White House endorsements. "It doesn't make sense to me," Accomondo said. Tinker stated, "I think she's lost a lot of ground and a lot of credibility as a Republican candidate." Both emphasized putting the community first in their statements.

Democratic candidates Katherine Waldron and Mario Guzman issued similar statements. Waldron said District 6 needs focused leadership on traffic, neighborhood protection, quality education, and responsible growth. Guzman said residents deserve a candidate committed to public needs who will bring stability and minimize negativity. Across all candidates and voters, the main issues facing District 6 are development, traffic, and the emergence of AI data centers. Baxter responded in a statement saying the election is about people, not politics. The District 6 primary is August 18, with the general election in November.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach motorcyclist killed in Boynton Beach crash at high speed
cards.teaser: Albert Garcia, 28, of West Palm Beach was killed when his motorcycle struck a car at the intersection of Boynton Beach Boulevard and El Clair Ranch Road.
cards.body:
A 28-year-old West Palm Beach man was killed Friday morning in a crash involving a motorcycle and a car at the intersection of Boynton Beach Boulevard and El Clair Ranch Road, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. The crash happened around 7:08 a.m.

Investigators said Albert Garcia was riding a 2007 Kawasaki Ninja eastbound on Boynton Beach Boulevard at a high rate of speed as he approached the intersection. At the same time, a 2016 Kia Forte driven by a 39-year-old Boynton Beach man was stopped in the westbound lanes and attempting to make a left turn onto southbound El Clair Ranch Road. As the Kia began turning left, Garcia applied the motorcycle's brakes but did not have enough time or distance to avoid a collision. The motorcycle struck the passenger side of the Kia inside the intersection. Garcia was thrown from the motorcycle and landed a short distance southwest of the impact point. Rescue crews transported Garcia to Delray Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. The driver of the Kia was wearing a seatbelt and was not injured. Garcia was wearing a helmet.
